sources.source: Using COPY TO and COPY FROM (psycopg 3)

items.item: COPY is one of the most efficient ways to load data into PostgreSQL
psycopg exposes COPY through Cursor.copy(), writing rows with write_row()
the ADBC PostgreSQL driver executes queries, including bulk ingestion, using COPY internally rather than a separate wire protocol
the COPY optimization can be disabled with the adbc.postgresql.use_copy statement option

at.out: not asserted by any reveal; this topic measures the default path, not the opt-out

items.item: Opening a connection is measurably slower than reusing an open one — a pool's entire reason to exist is that gap, not a theoretical concern.
A pool size isn't guessed — Little's Law (pool size = throughput × hold time) turns a measured hold time and a target throughput into a concrete number.
A SQL-level PREPARE/EXECUTE is forwarded straight to the physical backend connection, not tracked by PgBouncer unless max_prepared_statements is configured.
Under transaction pooling, a backend is returned to the pool the moment a transaction ends — even the same client's own next transaction isn't guaranteed that same backend.

items.item: A prepared statement lives on the physical backend, not the logical client connection — that's exactly what transaction pooling's backend-sharing exposes.
Session pooling avoids the prepared-statement caveat entirely by giving each client one dedicated backend for its whole connection, at the cost of not sharing that backend with anyone else meanwhile.

items.item: A server-side cursor trades server-side memory for the ability to process a result that wouldn't fit on the client at once, fetched in tuned batches instead of all at once.

items.item: Row-by-row inserts (executemany) are the slowest of the three bulk paths measured; COPY is the fastest.

An Arrow-native driver like ADBC isn't a different wire protocol for bulk loads — by its own documentation it runs COPY underneath, which is why its measured time tracks COPY's rather than executemany's.
Little's Law describes long-term averages; it doesn't size a pool correctly for bursty traffic, which still needs headroom beyond the formula's answer.
